newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Mir -- small name but big space station.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Mir -- small name but big space station.

text.p: Russia's troubled Mir space station is a cluttered amalgam of cylindrical modules and solar panels that has been assembled and reconfigured like a giant children's construction set circling high above the Earth.

Russian space officials said on Wednesday that Mir faced power problems and a partial pressure loss after its Spektr science module collided with an unmanned cargo craft during a manual docking exercise.
But they said the crew were not in immediate danger.

From an original 20-tonne Soviet-era building block launched in February 1986, Mir has become a sprawling space station that has received dozens of Soviet, Russian and foreign cosmonauts as well as U.S. astronauts. So far it has never been left unmanned.
There are now three men aboard Mir -- British-born U.S. astronaut Michael Foale and Russian cosmonauts Vasily Tsibilyev and Alexander Lazutkin.
The cosmonauts reached Mir -- the name means "world" and "peace" in Russian -- in February and were joined by Foale during a link-up with the U.S. space shuttle Atlantis in May.
The crew normally have the run of half a dozen modules with science-fiction names like Kvant-1, Priroda, Kristall, and including the Spektr unit involved in Wednesday's collision.

The core section is painted a mixture of white and homely pastel shades inside. There is even carpet because, despite the absence of gravity, crew members prefer to see a "floor" and "ceiling". Each cosmonaut has a tiny cabin with porthole.
The 12-metre (40-foot) Spektr module joined the station in May 1995 and contains U.S. and Russian scientific equipment for Earth observation and geophysical and atmospheric experiments.

Docked at right-angles to the core unit, Spektr has a conical end and four solar panels that fan out from its back -- one of the arrays was damaged in the collision and is robbing the station of vital power. Russian mission control also said there was a hole in the module body.

The Progress cargo tug that hit Spektr is one of many similar disposable craft sent up to replenish Mir periodically with anything from water and food to letters for the crew. Mission control said the seven-tonne tug had drifted away from Mir and would fall into the Pacific Ocean on Friday.
Back up in space, the Mir station's other modules all have longer term but varied roles, according to Russian and NASA information.

Kvant-1 was added 10 years ago to help cosmonauts study the galaxies while Kvant-2, sent up in 1989 and originally designed for a military space station that never materialised, provides life support systems and an airlock for space walks.

In 1990, the Soviet Union berthed the weighty Kristall module next to Kvant-2. Kristall, nearly as heavy as the core section, is used for producing materials in weightless conditions and biological tests.

The U.S. space shuttle Atlantis carried up a special module to clip on to Kristall in November 1995, offering a permanent docking port for its visits to the station. Other shuttles cannot dock with Mir.
The last module added to Mir was Priroda in April last year. It is used to monitor the Earth's ecology.

The final piece of the construction set is probably the most important -- the tiny Soyuz-TM spacecraft kept in place at one end of the station as an emergency lifeboat should the crew need to abandon ship and return to Earth in a hurry.
